p.src: Now Sima Yi heard that Cao Shuang, together with his brothers Cao Xi, Cao Xun, and Cao Yan, his confidants He Yan, Deng Yang, Ding Mi, Bi Fan, and Li Sheng, and the Imperial Guard, had accompanied the Wei emperor Cao Fang out of the city to pay homage at Emperor Ming's tomb and then gone hunting. Sima Yi was overjoyed. He immediately went to the government offices and ordered Minister over the Masses Gao Rou to assume the imperial insignia and battle-axe and act in the capacity of General-in-Chief, first seizing Cao Shuang's camp; he also ordered Grand Coachman Wang Guan to act as Commander of the Central Army and occupy Cao Xi's camp. Sima Yi led the former officials into the inner palace and memorialized Empress Dowager Guo, declaring that Cao Shuang had betrayed the late emperor's trust in entrusting him with the orphaned sovereign, and that his wickedness had thrown the realm into disorder, a crime for which he deserved dismissal. Empress Dowager Guo exclaimed in alarm, “The Son of Heaven is outside the city. What are we to do?” Sima Yi replied, “I have a memorial to present to His Majesty and a plan to execute the treacherous ministers. Your Majesty need not worry.” The empress dowager was afraid and had no choice but to consent. Sima Yi hastily ordered Grand Commandant Jiang Ji and Imperial Secretariat Director Sima Fu to compose a memorial together, then sent a palace attendant to carry it outside the city and present it directly before the emperor. Sima Yi himself led the main army and seized the arsenal. Word soon reached Cao Shuang's residence. His wife, Lady Liu, hurried into the front hall, summoned the officers guarding the residence, and asked, “Our lord is away. Why has Zhongda raised troops?” Pan Ju, the gate commander, said, “Do not be alarmed, my lady. I shall go and inquire.” He then led several dozen crossbowmen up the gate tower to look out. Just then he saw Sima Yi leading troops past the residence. Pan Ju ordered a volley of arrows shot down, preventing Sima Yi from passing. From behind, Deputy General Sun Qian stopped him, crying, “The Grand Tutor acts for a matter of state! Do not loose your arrows!” Only after he had stopped him three times did Pan Ju cease shooting. Sima Zhao guarded his father Sima Yi as they passed. They led the troops out of the city, encamped by the Luo River, and secured the pontoon bridge.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lu Zhi, an army major under Cao Shuang, saw the upheaval in the city and went to consult Staff Officer Xin Chang, saying, “Zhongda has now caused such turmoil. What are we to do?” Xin Chang replied, “We should lead our own troops out of the city and go before the Son of Heaven.” Lu Zhi agreed with him. Xin Chang hurried into the rear hall. His elder sister Xin Xianying saw him and asked, “What has happened that you are in such haste?” Xin Chang told her, “The Son of Heaven is outside the city, and the Grand Tutor has shut the gates. He must be plotting rebellion.” Xianying said, “Lord Sima is not necessarily plotting rebellion. He merely intends to kill General Cao.” Xin Chang exclaimed in surprise, “How can you know what will come of this?” Xianying replied, “General Cao is no match for Lord Sima. He will certainly be defeated.” Xin Chang said, “That day, the army major asked me to accompany him. I do not know whether I should go.” Xianying said, “Faithfulness to one's duty is a person's highest obligation. Even when an ordinary person falls into danger, one may still show him compassion. For one who holds his master's reins to abandon his duty would be the greatest ill omen of all.” Xin Chang followed her counsel. He and Lu Zhi led several dozen horsemen, cut their way through the barrier, seized the gate, and rode out.

p.src: Someone reported this to Sima Yi. Fearing that Huan Fan would also flee, Sima Yi urgently sent men to summon him. Huan Fan consulted with his son. His son said, “The imperial carriage is outside the city. We had better leave by the southern gate.” Huan Fan followed his advice, mounted his horse, and reached Pingchang Gate. The gate was already closed, and its commander, Si Fan, happened to be a former subordinate of Huan Fan. Huan Fan drew a bamboo tablet from his sleeve and said, “The empress dowager has issued an edict. Open the gate at once.” Si Fan said, “Please let me inspect the edict.” Huan Fan rebuked him, “You were once my subordinate! How dare you behave so?” Si Fan had no choice but to open the gate and let him out. Once outside the city, Huan Fan called back to Si Fan, “The Grand Tutor has rebelled! Make haste and come with me.” Si Fan was greatly alarmed, but when he pursued him, he could not catch up. Someone reported this to Sima Yi. Sima Yi exclaimed in alarm, “The brains of their cause have escaped! What are we to do?” Jiang Ji said, “A worn-out nag longs only for the beans in its stall; his counsel will surely go unheeded.” Sima Yi then summoned Xu Yun and Chen Tai and said, “Go and see Cao Shuang. Tell him that the Grand Tutor intends nothing else and merely wishes to strip him and his brothers of their military authority.” Xu Yun and Chen Tai departed. He also summoned Yin Damu, Commandant of the Palace Guard; he had Jiang Ji write a letter and ordered Yin Damu to take it to Cao Shuang. Sima Yi instructed him, “You are close to Cao Shuang and can undertake this mission. When you see him, say that Jiang Ji and I swear by the Luo River that this concerns only his military authority and that we have no other intent.” Yin Damu departed in obedience to the order.

p.src: When the Wei emperor Cao Fang had finished listening, he summoned Cao Shuang and said, “Such are the Grand Tutor's words. How do you intend to deal with this?” Cao Shuang was utterly at a loss. Turning to his two younger brothers, he asked, “What are we to do?” Cao Xi said, “Your unworthy younger brother once remonstrated with you, but you stubbornly refused to listen, and so matters have come to this. Sima Yi's cunning and deceit are beyond compare. Even Kongming could not defeat him; how could we brothers hope to do so? We had better bind ourselves and go before him, that we may escape death.” Before he had finished speaking, Staff Officer Xin Chang and Army Major Lu Zhi arrived. Cao Shuang questioned them. They told him, “The city is sealed as tightly as an iron barrel, and the Grand Tutor has led troops to encamp at the pontoon bridge over the Luo River. It appears impossible to return. You must decide upon a great plan at once.” While they were speaking, Minister of Agriculture Huan Fan arrived at a gallop and said to Cao Shuang, “The Grand Tutor has launched a coup. Why do you not ask the Son of Heaven to proceed to the capital at Xu, summon the troops outside the city, and campaign against Sima Yi?” Cao Shuang said, “Our entire families are in the city. How could we go elsewhere to seek reinforcements?” Huan Fan said, “Even a common man facing disaster still hopes to survive! Now, my lord, you accompany the Son of Heaven and can issue commands throughout the realm. Who would dare not respond? How can you cast yourself into a place of certain death?”

p.src: Cao Shuang heard him but could not decide; he did nothing but shed tears. Huan Fan said again, “The journey from here to the capital at Xu takes no more than half a night. The grain and fodder in the city are sufficient for several years. The troops of your separate camp, my lord, are close by to the south of the palace; summon them, and they will come at once. I have brought the seal of the Grand Marshal with me. You must depart at once, my lord. If you delay, all is lost!” Cao Shuang said, “Gentlemen, do not press me so hard. Let me consider the matter carefully.” A short while later, Palace Attendant Xu Yun and Imperial Secretariat Director Chen Tai arrived. The two told him, “The Grand Tutor acts only because your authority is too great, General. He merely wishes to remove your military command and has no other intent. You should return to the city at once.” Cao Shuang remained silent. Then Commandant of the Palace Guard Yin Damu was seen approaching. Yin Damu said, “The Grand Tutor has sworn by the Luo River that he has no other intent. I have here a letter from Grand Commandant Jiang. You need only relinquish your military authority, General, and return to your ministerial residence at once.” Cao Shuang believed this to be sound counsel. Huan Fan warned him again, “The situation is desperate! Do not listen to outsiders and walk into a place of certain death!”

p.src: That night Cao Shuang could not make up his mind. Sword in hand, he sighed and pondered; from dusk until dawn he wept without cease, yet remained irresolute. Huan Fan entered his tent and pressed him: “My lord has pondered for a day and a night. Why can you still not decide?” Shuang flung down his sword and sighed: “I will not raise troops. I shall ask only to relinquish office; it will be enough to live as a wealthy gentleman!” Huan Fan burst into tears and, leaving the tent, cried: “Cao Zidan prided himself on his wisdom and strategy, yet these three brothers are truly no better than piglets and calves!” He continued to weep bitterly. Xu Yun and Chen Tai urged Shuang first to surrender his seals and ribbons of office to Sima Yi. Shuang ordered the seals sent over. His registrar Yang Zong seized the seals and ribbons and wept: “My lord, if today you surrender military command, bind yourself, and go to submit, you cannot escape execution in the Eastern Market.” Shuang said, “The Grand Tutor will surely not break faith with me.” Cao Shuang then handed his seals and ribbons to Xu Yun and Chen Tai, who carried them ahead to Sima Yi. When the soldiers saw that their commander no longer had his seals, they all scattered. Only a few mounted officers remained with Shuang. When they reached the pontoon bridge, Yi issued orders that Cao Shuang and his two brothers were for the present to return to their private residences; all the others were to be imprisoned pending an imperial decree. When Shuang and the others entered the city, not a single attendant accompanied them. When Huan Fan reached the pontoon bridge, Yi pointed at him with his riding whip and said from horseback, “Minister Huan, why have you acted thus?” Huan Fan lowered his head without a word and entered the city.

p.src: Sima Yi then invited the emperor to strike camp and return to Luoyang. After Cao Shuang and his two brothers returned home, Yi secured their gates with great locks and ordered eight hundred local residents to surround and guard the residence. Cao Shuang was deeply troubled. Cao Xi said to him, “There is little grain left in the house. Elder brother, write to the Grand Tutor and ask to borrow some. If he is willing to lend us grain, he surely has no intention of harming us.” Shuang accordingly wrote a letter and sent someone to deliver it. Sima Yi read the letter and sent a hundred hu of grain to Cao Shuang’s residence. Shuang rejoiced: “Lord Sima truly has no intention of harming me!” Thereafter he ceased to worry.

p.src: In fact, Sima Yi had first arrested the palace eunuch Zhang Dang, imprisoned him, and interrogated him. Zhang Dang said, “I was not alone. He Yan, Deng Yang, Li Sheng, Bi Fan, and Ding Mi also conspired with me to usurp the throne and rebel.” Yi took Zhang Dang’s deposition, then arrested He Yan and the others and subjected them to a full inquiry. All confessed that they had intended to rebel in the third month. Yi had them nailed into long wooden cangues. Si Fan, the officer guarding the city gate, reported that Huan Fan had forged an imperial command to leave the city and had openly declared that the Grand Tutor was plotting rebellion. Yi said, “One who falsely accuses another of treason shall suffer the penalty for treason himself.” He also cast Huan Fan and the others into prison. Then Cao Shuang, his two brothers, and all their fellow prisoners were taken to the execution ground in the marketplace and beheaded, and their three clans were exterminated; all their property and valuables were confiscated and placed in the treasury. At that time, the wife of Cao Shuang’s cousin Wenshu was the daughter of Xiahou Ling. Widowed young and childless, she was pressed by her father to remarry, but cut off an ear to affirm her resolve. After Cao Shuang was executed, her father again tried to marry her to another, whereupon she cut off her nose as well. Her family was appalled and said to her, “Human life in this world is like a mote of dust resting on a frail blade of grass. Why torment yourself so cruelly? Moreover, the Sima clan has slaughtered your husband’s entire family. For whom do you mean to preserve your fidelity?” She wept and replied, “I have heard it said: ‘The benevolent do not alter their principles with prosperity or decline; the righteous do not change their hearts for life or death.’ Even when the Cao clan flourished, I wished to remain faithful to the end; now that it has perished, how could I bear to abandon it? Such conduct would befit beasts. How could I do it?” When Yi heard of this, he esteemed her virtue and permitted her to adopt and rear a son to continue the Cao line. A later poet wrote:

p.src: Now the Wei emperor Cao Fang appointed Sima Yi Chancellor and granted him the Nine Bestowments. Yi steadfastly declined and would not accept them. Cao Fang refused his resignation and ordered Yi and his two sons jointly to manage the affairs of state. Suddenly Yi reflected: “Though Cao Shuang’s whole family has been executed, Xiahou Ba still guards Yong Province and the surrounding districts. He is Cao Shuang’s kinsman; if he suddenly rebels, how are we to guard against him? He must be dealt with.” He immediately sent an imperial summons to Yong Province, ordering General Who Conquers the West Xiahou Ba to come to Luoyang to discuss affairs. When Xiahou Ba heard of this, he was greatly alarmed and at once led the three thousand troops under his command in revolt. Guo Huai, Inspector of Yong Province, learned of Xiahou Ba’s revolt and led his own troops to engage him. Guo Huai rode forth and reviled him: “You are a member of the imperial house of Great Wei, and the Son of Heaven has never wronged you. Why have you rebelled?” Xiahou Ba retorted: “My forefathers rendered many distinguished services to the state. What sort of man is Sima Yi, that he should exterminate my Cao kindred and now come to seize me? Sooner or later he will surely seek to usurp the throne. I uphold righteousness and punish a traitor—how can that be called rebellion?” Guo Huai flew into a rage, leveled his spear, and spurred his horse straight at Xiahou Ba. Xiahou Ba brandished his saber and galloped forward to meet him. Before ten bouts had passed, Guo Huai turned and fled, with Xiahou Ba pursuing close behind. Suddenly shouts rose from the rear. As Xiahou Ba hastily wheeled his horse around, Chen Tai came charging up with his troops. Guo Huai then turned back. Attacked from both sides, Xiahou Ba suffered a crushing defeat and fled, losing more than half his troops; unable to devise any other course, he fled to Hanzhong and surrendered to the Later Ruler.

Yi steadfastly declined and would not accept them.
Cao Fang refused his resignation and ordered Yi and his two sons jointly to manage the affairs of state.

Suddenly Yi reflected: “Though Cao Shuang’s whole family has been executed, Xiahou Ba still guards Yong Province and the surrounding districts. He is Cao Shuang’s kinsman; if he suddenly rebels, how are we to guard against him?
He must be dealt with.”
He immediately sent an imperial summons to Yong Province, ordering General Who Conquers the West Xiahou Ba to come to Luoyang to discuss affairs.
When Xiahou Ba heard of this, he was greatly alarmed and at once led the three thousand troops under his command in revolt.
Guo Huai, Inspector of Yong Province, learned of Xiahou Ba’s revolt and led his own troops to engage him.
Guo Huai rode forth and reviled him: “You are a member of the imperial house of Great Wei, and the Son of Heaven has never wronged you. Why have you rebelled?”

Xiahou Ba retorted: “My forefathers rendered many distinguished services to the state. What sort of man is Sima Yi, that he should exterminate my Cao kindred and now come to seize me? Sooner or later he will surely seek to usurp the throne.
I uphold righteousness and punish a traitor—how can that be called rebellion?”
Guo Huai flew into a rage, leveled his spear, and spurred his horse straight at Xiahou Ba.
Xiahou Ba brandished his saber and galloped forward to meet him.
Before ten bouts had passed, Guo Huai turned and fled, with Xiahou Ba pursuing close behind.
Suddenly shouts rose from the rear. As Xiahou Ba hastily wheeled his horse around, Chen Tai came charging up with his troops.
Guo Huai then turned back.
Attacked from both sides, Xiahou Ba suffered a crushing defeat and fled, losing more than half his troops;
unable to devise any other course, he fled to Hanzhong and surrendered to the Later Ruler.

p.src: Someone reported the matter to Jiang Wei, but he did not believe it. Only after sending men to investigate and verify the truth did he order that Xiahou Ba be admitted into the city. After paying his respects, Xiahou Ba tearfully recounted all that had happened. Jiang Wei said, “Long ago, when Weizi abandoned Zhou, he won undying renown. If you can help restore the House of Han, you will be no less worthy than the men of old.” He then gave a banquet in Xiahou Ba’s honor. Once they were seated, Jiang Wei asked, “Now that Sima Yi and his sons wield supreme power, do they intend to encroach upon our realm?” Xiahou Ba replied, “The old traitor is now plotting rebellion and has no leisure to concern himself with foreign states. But two young men have lately arisen in Wei. If they are placed in command of armies, they will pose a grave threat to both Wu and Shu.” Jiang Wei asked, “Who are these two men?” Xiahou Ba told him, “One presently serves as a Gentleman of the Palace Writers and is a native of Changshe in Yingchuan. His surname is Zhong, his given name Hui, and his courtesy name Shiji. He is the son of Grand Tutor Zhong Yao. From childhood he possessed courage and intelligence. Zhong Yao once took his two sons to an audience with Emperor Wen. Hui was then seven years old, while his elder brother Yu was eight. At the sight of the emperor, Yu became so terrified that sweat streamed over his face. The emperor asked Yu, ‘Why are you sweating?’ Yu replied, ‘I tremble in awe and dread, and my sweat pours forth like water.’ The emperor then asked Hui, ‘Why are you not sweating?’ Hui replied, ‘I tremble with fear, and my sweat dares not come forth.’ The emperor considered him extraordinary. As he grew older, he delighted in reading military treatises and gained a profound understanding of strategy. Both Sima Yi and Jiang Ji praised his talent. The other presently serves as a minor official and is a native of Yiyang. His surname is Deng, his given name Ai, and his courtesy name Shizai. He lost his father in childhood and always harbored lofty ambitions. Whenever he saw lofty mountains or broad marshes, he would survey the terrain and point out where troops might be stationed, provisions stored, and ambushes laid. Everyone laughed at him, but Sima Yi alone recognized his exceptional talent and appointed him to assist in military planning. Deng Ai stammered, and whenever he made a report he would begin, ‘Ai... Ai...’ Sima Yi once teased him, saying, ‘You keep saying “Ai, Ai”; how many Ais are there?’ Deng Ai instantly replied, ‘When one says, “O phoenix, O phoenix,” there is still only one phoenix.’ Such was the quickness of his natural wit. These two men are greatly to be feared.” Jiang Wei laughed and said, “They are mere boys. They are hardly worth mentioning!”

p.src: Jiang Wei then escorted Xiahou Ba to Chengdu and brought him before the Latter Lord. Jiang Wei memorialized, “Sima Yi plotted the murder of Cao Shuang and then sought to lure Xiahou Ba into a trap, so Xiahou Ba has come over to us. Now Sima Yi and his sons monopolize power, while Cao Fang is weak; the state of Wei will soon be imperiled. I have been stationed in Hanzhong for years; our troops are well trained and our provisions abundant. I beg leave to command Your Majesty’s army, appoint Xiahou Ba as my guide, advance upon the Central Plains, restore the House of Han, repay Your Majesty’s grace, and fulfill the late Chancellor’s ambition.” Fei Yi, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, remonstrated, “Recently Jiang Wan and Dong Yun have died one after the other, leaving no one to manage our domestic government. Boyue should await the proper time and not act rashly.” Jiang Wei said, “I disagree. A man’s life passes as swiftly as a white colt glimpsed through a crack. If we keep letting the years slip by, when shall we ever recover the Central Plains?” Fei Yi said further, “Sun Tzu says, ‘Know the enemy and know yourself, and you will win every battle.’ All of us fall far short of the Chancellor. Even he could not recover the Central Plains—how much less can we?” Jiang Wei said, “I lived long in the Longxi region and know the hearts of the Qiang people well. If we now ally ourselves with the Qiang, then even if we cannot recover the Central Plains, we can seize and hold all the territory west of Long.” The Latter Lord said, “Since you wish to campaign against Wei, devote all your loyalty and strength to it. Do not lose your keen resolve and thereby fail the charge I entrust to you.” Jiang Wei accordingly received the imperial decree and took leave of the court. Together with Xiahou Ba, he went straight to Hanzhong to plan the campaign. Jiang Wei said, “First we should send an envoy to make an alliance with the Qiang, then march from Xiping toward Yong Province. We shall first build two fortresses below Mount Qu and station troops in them, so that they support each other like the two horns of a beast. We shall bring all our provisions to the mouth of the valley and, following the late Chancellor’s system, advance the army in successive stages.” In the eighth month of that autumn, the Shu generals Gou An and Li Xin were sent ahead with fifteen thousand troops to build two adjoining fortresses before Mount Qu. Gou An guarded the eastern fortress, and Li Xin the western.

p.src: Spies soon reported this to Guo Huai, Inspector of Yong Province. Guo Huai reported the matter to Luoyang while also dispatching his deputy, Chen Tai, with fifty thousand troops to engage the Shu army at Mount Qu. Gou An and Li Xin each led a force out to meet him. But being too few to withstand the enemy, they withdrew into their fortresses. Chen Tai ordered his troops to surround and assault the fortresses from all sides, while another force cut their supply route from Hanzhong. Provisions began to run short within the fortresses held by Gou An and Li Xin. Guo Huai then arrived in person with another army. After examining the terrain, he was delighted. Returning to camp, he conferred with Chen Tai: “These fortresses stand upon high ground, so they must lack water and have to send men outside to fetch it. If we block the upstream flow, all the Shu soldiers will die of thirst.” He therefore ordered his soldiers to dig earth and dam the upper stream. As expected, there was soon no water inside the fortresses. Li Xin led troops out to fetch water, but the Yong Province army closed around them fiercely. Though Li Xin fought desperately, he could not break through and had no choice but to retreat into the fortress. Gou An’s fortress was likewise without water, so he joined Li Xin and led his troops out, combining their forces. After a long battle, they were defeated once more and driven back into the fortresses. The soldiers were parched with thirst. Gou An and Li Xin said, “Commander Jiang’s army has still not arrived. We do not know why.” Li Xin said, “I shall risk my life, break through, and seek help.” He then took several dozen horsemen, opened the fortress gate, and charged out. The Yong Province troops converged upon him from every side. Li Xin fought furiously and only just managed to break free. In the end he alone escaped, grievously wounded; all the others perished amid the melee. That night a strong north wind arose, dark clouds gathered, and heavy snow fell from the sky. Thus the Shu troops inside the fortresses rationed their provisions and melted snow for sustenance.

p.src: Now Li Xin, having fought his way out of the encirclement, traveled for two days along a narrow path through the western hills and came upon Jiang Wei’s army. Li Xin dismounted, prostrated himself, and reported, “Both fortresses at Mount Qu are surrounded by the Wei army, which has cut off their water supply. Fortunately, heavy snow fell from the sky, so the men have survived by melting it. Their situation is extremely perilous.” Jiang Wei said, “I did not delay their rescue intentionally. The Qiang troops I was assembling have not yet arrived, and that has held me up.” He then ordered that Li Xin be sent into Shu to recover from his wounds. Jiang Wei asked Xiahou Ba, “The Qiang troops have not arrived, while the Wei army presses the siege of Mount Qu most fiercely. General, what wise counsel can you offer?” Xiahou Ba replied, “If we wait until the Qiang troops reach Mount Qu, both fortresses will already have fallen. I believe the troops of Yong Province must all have gone to attack Mount Qu. Yong Province’s capital must therefore be empty. You can lead the army straight to Niutou Mountain and circle around behind it. Guo Huai and Chen Tai will surely turn back to rescue Yong Province, and the siege of Mount Qu will lift of itself.” Jiang Wei was delighted and said, “That is an excellent plan!” Jiang Wei then led his army toward Niutou Mountain.

p.src: Now when Chen Tai saw that Li Xin had fought his way out of the fortress, he said to Guo Huai, “If Li Xin reports the emergency to Jiang Wei, Jiang Wei will reckon that our main army is entirely at Mount Qu and will surely circle around Niutou Mountain to strike our rear. General, take one force and seize the Tao River, thereby cutting the Shu army’s supply route. I shall divide off half the troops and go straight to Niutou Mountain to attack him. When he learns that his supply route has been cut, he will certainly withdraw of his own accord.” Guo Huai followed this advice and secretly led a force to seize the Tao River. Chen Tai led another force straight toward Niutou Mountain.

p.src: Now Jiang Wei's army reached Mount Niutou, when suddenly shouts arose from the vanguard and a report came that the Wei army had blocked the road ahead. In alarm, Jiang Wei hurried forward to see for himself. Chen Tai shouted, “You mean to raid our province of Yong! I have been waiting for you a long while!” Enraged, Jiang Wei leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and charged straight at Chen Tai. Chen Tai brandished his saber and met him. Before three bouts had passed, Chen Tai turned and fled in defeat. Jiang Wei waved his troops forward in pursuit. The troops of Yongzhou fell back. They occupied the hilltop. Jiang Wei recalled his troops and made camp below Mount Niutou. Each day Jiang Wei sent troops to challenge the enemy, but neither side gained the upper hand. Xiahou Ba said to Jiang Wei, “This is no place to remain for long. Though we have fought for days without a decision, this is merely a scheme to lure our troops; they must have some hidden design. We would do better to withdraw for now and devise a sound plan anew.” Even as he spoke, a sudden report came that Guo Huai had led an army to seize the Tao River and cut their supply route. Jiang Wei was greatly alarmed and promptly ordered Xiahou Ba to withdraw first. Jiang Wei himself guarded the rear. Chen Tai divided his forces into five columns and came in pursuit. Jiang Wei alone held the junction of all five routes and checked the Wei troops. Chen Tai drove his troops up the mountain, while arrows and stones rained down. When Jiang Wei hastily retreated to the Tao River, Guo Huai led his troops in an attack. Jiang Wei led his troops in repeated charges back and forth. The Wei troops blocked his escape, packed as tightly as an iron barrel. Jiang Wei fought desperately and broke through, but lost more than half his troops, then raced toward Yangping Pass. Yet another army came charging from ahead; at its head, a great commander galloped forth with saber held crosswise. He had a round face, large ears, a square mouth, and thick lips. Beneath his left eye was a black growth bearing several dozen black hairs. This was Sima Yi's eldest son, Sima Shi, General of Agile Cavalry. Jiang Wei cried furiously, “How dare you, boy, bar my road home!” He spurred his horse, leveled his spear, and charged straight at Sima Shi. Sima Shi swung his saber and met the attack. In only three bouts Jiang Wei defeated Sima Shi, broke free, and made straight for Yangping Pass. The men upon the walls opened the gate and let Jiang Wei inside. Sima Shi also rushed forward to seize the pass, but concealed crossbows on both sides discharged together, each crossbow loosing ten bolts. This was the method of the “repeating crossbow” bequeathed by the Martial Marquis upon his death. As the verse says:
